docs.title: varTrack
docs.text: GitOps-native configuration sync. Push a file to Git — varTrack writes it to your datastores automatically.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
You commit a config file. varTrack syncs it everywhere.

# configs/app.yaml — lives in your Git repo
database_host: mongo.prod.internal
feature_flag_dark_mode: true
max_connections: 50

Push to main → varTrack automatically writes these values to every configured sink:

MongoDB     →  collection "production-config"
Redis       →  hash       "production:cfg"
ZooKeeper   →  znodes     /acme/production/
S3          →  key prefix acme/production/

If someone edits MongoDB directly and changes max_connections to 5, the watcher detects it and restores 50 automatically — no manual intervention needed.

docs.title: Why varTrack?
docs.text:
Git is a good home for application configuration, but the values your applications read live in datastores — MongoDB documents, Redis hashes, ZooKeeper znodes, S3 objects, Linux .env files — and nothing keeps them in step with Git.

varTrack fills that gap. It treats Git as the single source of truth for application configuration data, and writes it to the datastores your applications actually read.

varTrack Target MongoDB, Redis, ZooKeeper, S3, ConfigMap, Helm, Vercel, Linux Trigger Git push / webhook Drift detection Any datasource Secret management HashiCorp Vault integration Schema validation CUE schema per tenant

It works alongside whatever deploys your services: varTrack only keeps their runtime config in sync.

docs.title: Key features
docs.text:
• 8 sink types

    MongoDB, Redis, ZooKeeper, S3, Kubernetes ConfigMap, Helm, Vercel, Linux server (SSH)

    See all sinks

  • Secret management

    @secret() annotations pull values from HashiCorp Vault at ETL time. Secrets never touch Git. Dry-run reports mask them as ***

    Schema annotations

  • CUE schema validation

    Every push is validated against a per-tenant CUE schema before any write. Invalid configs are rejected with a detailed error — zero bad writes

    Schema annotations

  • Drift detection

    The watcher asks the orchestrator each poll whether a datasource still matches Git. On drift, it logs the delta and optionally restores correct state — automatically

    How drift detection works

  • Multi-sink fan-out

    One push writes to multiple sinks in parallel. One rule set for all environments

    Destination template

  • Any config format

    YAML, JSON, TOML, .env, INI, HCL, XML — format auto-detected from file extension

    Supported formats

  • CLI — vt

    Push any local file from terminal or CI/CD. Validate against schemas. Inspect tasks

    CLI reference

  • Dry-run mode

    Simulate any sync and see exactly what would be written — without touching a datasource. Secret fields masked as ***

    Dry-run reference

docs.title: Try it in one command
docs.text:
The fastest way to see varTrack in action is the end-to-end demo. It starts a local Git server, MongoDB, ZooKeeper, Redis, and all three varTrack services:

cd e2e
docker compose up

Push a config change to the local repo and watch it sync automatically.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    GIT["📁 Git repo\n(GitHub / Gitea / GitLab)"]
    GW["gateway-service\nGo · :5657"]
    ORCH["orchestrator-service\nPython · :50051\n─────────────\nRust ETL core"]
    WATCH["watcher-service\nGo · :9091"]

    GIT -->|"webhook\n(push / PR)"| GW
    GW -->|"gRPC\nProcessWebhook"| ORCH

    ORCH -->|write| MONGO["MongoDB"]
    ORCH -->|write| REDIS["Redis"]
    ORCH -->|write| ZK["ZooKeeper"]
    ORCH -->|write| S3["S3 / MinIO"]
    ORCH -->|write| OTHER["ConfigMap · Helm\nVercel · Linux"]

    WATCH -->|"CheckDatasource\n(drift check)"| ORCH
    WATCH -->|"SyncDatasource\n(self-heal)"| ORCH
  1. You push a config file.
  2. gateway-service (Go) receives the webhook, verifies the HMAC signature, and forwards it via gRPC.
  3. orchestrator-service (Python) fetches the file from Git, validates it against a CUE schema, runs the Rust ETL core (diff, merge, prune), and writes to all configured sinks.
  4. watcher-service (Go) asks the orchestrator on a configurable interval whether each self_heal rule's datasource still matches Git — the orchestrator reads the sink — and on drift has it restore correct state.

Why Rust inside the orchestrator?

The ETL core (diff, flatten, merge, prune) is implemented in Rust and called from Python via FFI. This keeps the hot path allocation-free and handles multi-megabyte config payloads without GC pressure, while the Python layer handles I/O, Vault, and sink drivers.

Full architecture overview

docs.title: Which file do I change?
docs.text:
To change Edit Owned by Which repositories are synced, where data goes, credentials, self_heal, what may never change (force) config.cue the team running varTrack A tenant's branches, root keys, prune and sync settings for the rules it uses the tenant's bundle.json the tenant One repository's settings its vartrack.json the repository's owners

Configuration files has the full picture, and Rule options which file may set each option.

docs.title: I changed config.cue — do I need to restart?
docs.text: The orchestrator re-reads it when the file changes. The gateway reads it once at startup: restart it after changing platforms, rules or repositories. The watcher reads it only for leader election.

docs.title: I changed bundle.json — when does it apply?
docs.text: At the next refresh of the tenant's schema repository: every SCHEMA_TTL_SECONDS (300 s), or at once on a push when the repository is the one config.cue's schema_registry names.

docs.title: Does vartrack.json on a feature branch apply?
docs.text: Yes, to pushes of that branch: the file is read at the pushed commit, so each branch can carry its own.

docs.title: What happens on a push to a branch I did not map?
docs.text: It is synced to the environment default. Map every branch you push to — see Environment resolution.

docs.title: Can a repository turn on self_heal, or change where data is written?
docs.text: No. self_heal, repositories, secret_manager, force, tenants and the datasources' connection settings come from config.cue only. A repository can set the options listed under Overridable keys, and force still wins.

docs.title: Will varTrack delete keys I added by hand?
docs.text: No. Prune deletes only keys varTrack wrote before and Git no longer holds, and keeps a key whose value something else changed since (with a PruneSkipped event). Keys matching a protection pattern are never deleted. See What prune deletes.

docs.title: Two datasources write the same Redis — will one prune the other's keys?
docs.text: No. Each sync records the key space it wrote to; a prune keeps every key another target holds in the same key space, and warns once with a SharedKeySpace event.

docs.title: How do I try a change without writing anything?
docs.text: vt sync --dry-run … (or dry_run: true in the rule) reads, validates and reports what would be written. prune: {enabled: true, dry_run: true} reports what prune would delete.

docs.title: Where are secrets kept?
docs.text: Not in Git. config.cue credentials can be {file: …} (a mounted secret) or {ref: …} (Vault); a config file's values can be @secret() fields its CUE schema marks, fetched from Vault when the file is synced. varTrack records only digests of secret values. See Secret value forms and Schema annotations.

docs.title: Why does the web UI not show a rule?
docs.text: The UI shows what your Git account can read. A rule whose repositories you cannot read, or whose platform you have not connected, is counted as hidden; Connect signs in to that platform. Without ui.auth, the UI shows every rule.

docs.title: Can I run several gateways, workers and watchers?
docs.text: Yes. Workers and gateways scale out; one watcher leads at a time. Set gateway_nonce_datasource and watcher_leader_election_datasource — see High availability.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: Get varTrack running locally in under 10 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Go 1.21+
  • Python 3.11+
  • A Celery broker — Redis or MongoDB (configured via celery_broker_datasource in the bundle)
  • At least one configured sink
  • buf CLI — for proto code generation

docs.title: Option A — E2E demo (fastest)
docs.text:
No manual setup needed. Starts everything in Docker:

git clone https://github.com/jarin-devoss/varTrack
cd varTrack/e2e
docker compose up

This starts a local Git server, MongoDB, ZooKeeper, Redis, and all three varTrack services with a pre-configured bundle. Push any config change to the local repo and watch it sync.

docs.title: With more sinks and the web UI
docs.text:
e2e/docker-compose.live.yml adds S3 on MinIO and Kubernetes ConfigMaps and Helm releases on k3s, and seeds every sink through real Gitea pushes and webhooks:

buf generate          # the orchestrator image needs the Python gRPC stubs
cd e2e
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.live.yml up -d --build \
  gitea redis mongo zookeeper minio minio-init vault vault-init \
  k3s k3s-kubeconfig orchestrator-api orchestrator-worker gateway watcher live-seed

cd ../ui && npm install && npm run dev

Open the UI at http://localhost:5173. Two Git servers feed the demo, so sign-in covers two platforms: gitea (http://localhost:3000, the demo configs) and gitea-team (http://127.0.0.1:3001, a payments team with a private repository). Sign in with one and connect the other — every password is VarTrack123:

Sign in to gitea as… then connect gitea-team as… you see demo-admin team-admin all 7 rules on one page, and can sync them: the 6 demo rules of tenant default and the payments rule of tenant payments, with no tenant to switch to demo-viewer demo-viewer the 6 demo rules, dry runs only; the payments rule stays hidden — not in that team

The demo's rule settings come in layers (how a rule is built):

Layer In the demo config.cue e2e/live/config.cue: every rule, the datasources' connections, Vault a tenant's bundle.json tenant default: vartrack-demo/schemas on gitea, extends the production preset · tenant payments: payments/schemas on gitea-team, extends the team preset on gitea a repo's vartrack.json demo-configs has one on main and a different one on develop; payments-config has .gitea/vartrack.json, extending a preset in the payments team's own schema repo presets vartrack-demo/presets (e2e/live/presets): each layer adds prune.protection patterns

Every environment shows its desired state in Git next to the current state in its sink. See Web UI sign-in to turn sign-in off or set it up for your own platforms.

docs.title: 1. Clone and generate proto code
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/jarin-devoss/varTrack
cd varTrack
buf generate

docs.title: 2. Write config.cue
docs.text:
All three services share one CUE bundle that declares your platforms, datasources, and rules.

bundle: {
  platforms: [{
    github: {
      endpoint:        "https://github.com"
      push_event_name: "push"
      pr_event_name:   "pull_request"
      secret:          "my-webhook-secret"
    }
  }]

  datasources: [{
    mongo: {
      endpoint:   "mongodb://localhost:27017"
      database:   "vartrack"
      collection: "variables"
    }
  }]

  rules: [{
    platform:             "github"
    datasource:           "mongo"
    file_name:            "configs/app.yaml"   // file to watch in each repo
    repositories:         ["my-org/*"]         // glob — which repos trigger this rule
    destination_template: "{env}-config"       // collection name resolved at sync time
    self_heal:            true
    branch_map: {
      main:    "production"
      develop: "staging"
    }
  }]
}

docs.title: 3. Start the gateway-service
docs.text:
APP_ENV=dev \
ORCHESTRATOR_ADDR=localhost:50051 \
CONFIG_PATH=config.cue \
go run ./gateway-service/cmd

Listens on :5657 (webhooks) and :9090 (metrics/health).

docs.title: 4. Start the orchestrator-service
docs.text:
cd orchestrator-service
pip install -e .

# API + gRPC server
uvicorn main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 &

# Celery worker (separate terminal)
celery -A app.worker.celery worker --queues=webhooks,sync -l info

docs.title: 5. Start the watcher-service
docs.text:
ORCHESTRATOR_ADDR=localhost:50051 \
CONFIG_PATH=config.cue \
go run ./watcher-service/cmd

Every 60 seconds by default, asks the orchestrator whether each self_heal rule's datasource still matches Git.

docs.title: 6. Register a webhook in GitHub
docs.text:
Point your repository webhook to http://your-server:5657/webhooks/mongo:

Setting Value Payload URL http://your-server:5657/webhooks/mongo Content type application/json Secret Value of secret from config.cue Events Pushes + Pull requests

Every push to a matching repository now triggers a sync automatically.

docs.title: Verify it works
docs.text:
Push a change to a tracked repository, then check MongoDB:

mongosh vartrack --eval 'db["production-config"].find().pretty()'

You should see your config values written as key-value documents.

docs.title: Install the CLI
docs.text:
The vt CLI lets you sync files directly without a Git push:

cd cli
go build -o vt ./cmd
mv vt /usr/local/bin/vt

# Authenticate with your Git token (GitHub or Gitea)
vt login --server http://localhost:5657 --token <your Git token>

# Push a file manually
vt sync --file configs/app.yaml --datasource mongo --env staging --wait

What vt may do is what your Git token may do in the rule's repositories: push access syncs, read access validates and dry-runs — see Authentication & Authorization. In the live demo, make a Gitea token and use it:

TOKEN=$(curl -s -u demo-admin:VarTrack123 -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"vt","scopes":["read:user","read:repository"]}' \
  http://localhost:3000/api/v1/users/demo-admin/tokens | python3 -c "import sys,json;print(json.load(sys.stdin)['sha1'])")
vt login --server http://localhost:5657 --token "$TOKEN"
vt sync --file app-settings.yaml --datasource mongo-primary --env staging --wait   # the live demo's rule tracks app-settings.yaml

demo-admin administers the demo repositories, so it can sync anywhere; demo-viewer can only read them, so it can validate and dry-run but not sync (the example OPA policy adds: writers never sync production or configs/secrets/*). The same token, pasted under API token for the Playground on the UI's sign-in page, drives the Playground.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Most teams manage runtime configuration through one of two approaches — and both have serious weaknesses.

Direct database edits

  • No audit trail — who changed max_connections from 50 to 5 at 3 AM?
  • Changes are invisible to the rest of the team
  • Drift goes undetected until something breaks
  • No validation — typos and bad values go straight to production

Scattered .env and config files

  • Duplicated across repos and deployment scripts
  • Environments drift out of sync silently
  • No single place to see what is deployed where
  • Secrets baked into files or CI variables with no rotation story

docs.title: The Git-as-source-of-truth model
docs.text:
varTrack treats your Git repository as the single authority for configuration data:

  • Every change is a commit — full audit trail, PR review, rollback
  • Push to main → production synced; push to develop → staging synced
  • Invalid configs are rejected before any write (CUE schema validation)
  • Drift is caught within one poll interval and optionally healed automatically

docs.title: What varTrack syncs
docs.text:
varTrack syncs configuration data, not Kubernetes resources.

varTrack What it syncs Configuration data: MongoDB, Redis, ZooKeeper, S3, ConfigMap, Helm values, Vercel env vars, Linux files Where config lives The application's own datastore Drift detection Any datasource — MongoDB, Redis, ZooKeeper, S3 Secret management HashiCorp Vault with @secret() annotations Schema validation CUE schema per tenant, enforced before every write Targets Redis, MongoDB, ZooKeeper, S3, Linux SSH, Vercel, ConfigMap, Helm Multi-sink fan-out One push → multiple sinks in parallel

It works alongside whatever deploys your services. A typical setup:

Git push
  ├── your deployment pipeline → deploys your services
  └── varTrack → syncs runtime config into MongoDB + Redis + ConfigMap

docs.title: How it compares to HashiCorp Consul
docs.text:
Consul is a service mesh and distributed KV store. It doesn't help you get config into Consul from Git, validate it, or fan it out to other systems.

varTrack can write to Consul (via ZooKeeper-compatible API or directly), with full Git history, schema validation, drift detection, and multi-env routing.

docs.title: How it compares to manual Helm values
docs.text:
Helm values files in Git are a common pattern, but they have limitations:

  • Values are only applied on helm upgrade — no continuous reconciliation
  • No fan-out to non-Helm sinks (MongoDB, Redis, etc.)
  • No runtime drift detection — if someone kubectl edits the ConfigMap, nobody knows

varTrack's Helm sink triggers helm upgrade on push and the watcher can detect if the deployed values diverge from what Git says.

docs.title: When varTrack is the right fit
docs.text:
✅ You store config, feature flags, or environment variables in MongoDB, Redis, S3, ZooKeeper, ConfigMaps, Helm releases, Vercel, or Linux servers — and want Git as the single authority

✅ You have multiple environments (dev, staging, production) and want changes to flow automatically on push without manual scripts

✅ You need drift detection — if someone edits a value directly in any sink, varTrack restores the correct state

✅ You want secrets to stay in Vault and never touch Git — @secret() annotations resolve at sync time

✅ You need to validate configs before they reach the datastore — CUE schemas catch bad values at the gate

docs.title: When varTrack is NOT the right fit
docs.text:
❌ You only need to sync Kubernetes manifests — a deployment tool is the better fit

❌ You want a general-purpose feature flag service (LaunchDarkly, Unleash) with gradual rollouts and targeting rules

❌ Your config is too dynamic to live in Git (e.g. user-generated content, real-time game state)

docs.title: vt — CLI Reference
docs.text: vt is the command-line interface for varTrack. Push any local config file directly to a datasource from your terminal or CI/CD pipeline — without needing a Git push.

docs.title: Download pre-built binary
docs.text: Download from the releases page for your platform, then add to your PATH.

docs.title: Build from source
docs.text:
cd cli
go build -o vt ./cmd
mv vt /usr/local/bin/vt

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
vt authenticates with your Git token — a GitHub or Gitea personal access token. What it may do is what that token may do in the rule's repositories: push access syncs, read access validates and dry-runs (Authentication & Authorization).

vt login --server https://gateway.example.com --token "$GIT_TOKEN"

# Or skip login entirely — set env vars
export VARTRACK_SERVER=https://gateway.example.com
export VARTRACK_TOKEN=<your Git token>

docs.title: vt sync
docs.text:
Push a local file to a datasource. Runs the full ETL pipeline.

# Basic sync
vt sync \
  --file       configs/app.yaml \
  --datasource mongo \
  --env        production

# Dry-run — see what would be written without touching the datasource
vt sync --file configs/app.yaml --datasource mongo --env staging --dry-run

# Wait for the task to complete
vt sync --file configs/app.yaml --datasource mongo --env production --wait

# Custom timeout and label
vt sync \
  --file       configs/app.yaml \
  --datasource mongo \
  --env        production \
  --wait       \
  --timeout    10m \
  --label      "release/v2.3.1"

# Output raw JSON
vt sync --file configs/app.yaml --datasource mongo --env staging --json

Flags:

Flag Default Description --file — Path to the config file (required) --datasource — Target datasource name (required) --platform — Platform of the rule (for example github, gitea-internal); needed only when rules on several platforms write to the datasource --env — Deployment environment (required) --tenant from context Tenant ID --dry-run false Validate without writing --wait false Block until task completes --timeout 5m Max wait time --label "" Free-form label attached to the task --json false Print raw JSON response

docs.title: vt validate
docs.text:
Validate a file against the CUE schema without syncing. Exits with code 1 on failure — ideal for PR checks.

vt validate --file configs/app.yaml

# Specify the datasource to select the right schema
vt validate --file configs/app.yaml --datasource mongo

# With tenant
vt validate --file configs/app.yaml --datasource mongo --tenant myapp

Flags:

Flag Default Description --file — Path to the config file (required) --datasource — Datasource name (selects the schema) --platform — Platform of the rule; needed only when rules on several platforms write to the datasource --tenant from context Tenant ID --format auto File format override --json false Print result as JSON

docs.title: vt validate-config
docs.text:
Check a vartrack.json or a tenant's bundle.json before pushing it, with the code a sync reads it with. With no file named, it checks the vartrack.json files in the current directory (vartrack.json, .github/vartrack.json, .gitea/vartrack.json, .gitlab/vartrack.json); with none, it prints no vartrack.json found and exits 0.

It exits with code 1 when any file has errors or warnings, and with --strict also when a file has migrations.

vt validate-config
vt validate-config --strict
vt validate-config vartrack.json
vt validate-config .gitea/vartrack.json
vt validate-config schemas/bundle.json --tenant payments

The file's name says what it is: vartrack.json (also under .github/, .gitea/ or .gitlab/), bundle.json or rules.json.

It reports What it means errors what a sync rejects: invalid JSON, a value of the wrong type, a second rule for one platform and datasource, a rule config.cue does not have or a tenant may not layer warnings what a sync ignores: keys only config.cue sets, removed options, prune that has no effect on a whole-object sink migrations options under a name that changed (env_as_branch → branch_as_env); a sync still reads them

A vartrack.json's extends presets are checked by name, not fetched. A bundle.json's presets are fetched from the tenant's schema repository, as a sync does.

Flags:

Flag Default Description --tenant from context Tenant ID: whose rules and presets a bundle.json is checked against --strict false Also exit 1 when a file uses options under a name that changed (migrations) --json false Print [{file, errors, warnings, migrations}] as JSON

The caller needs a token any platform of the bundle accepts; the file names no rule, so no repository permission is asked.

docs.title: CI/CD Integration
docs.text: Use vt in your pipeline to validate config files on every PR and sync on every merge.

docs.title: Recommended workflow
docs.text:
A typical CI/CD setup uses two steps:

  1. On pull request — validate the config file against the CUE schema. Block the PR if validation fails.
  2. On merge to main — sync the config to the production datasource.

docs.title: Validate on PR + sync on merge
docs.text:
name: Config sync

on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "configs/**"
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths:
      - "configs/**"

jobs:
  validate:
    name: Validate config
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Download vt
        run: |
          curl -sSL https://github.com/jarin-devoss/varTrack/releases/latest/download/vt_linux_amd64 \
            -o /usr/local/bin/vt && chmod +x /usr/local/bin/vt

      - name: Validate
        env:
          VARTRACK_SERVER: ${{ vars.VARTRACK_SERVER }}
          VARTRACK_TOKEN:  ${{ secrets.VARTRACK_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          vt validate --file configs/app.yaml --datasource mongo
          vt validate-config

  sync:
    name: Sync to production
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Download vt
        run: |
          curl -sSL https://github.com/jarin-devoss/varTrack/releases/latest/download/vt_linux_amd64 \
            -o /usr/local/bin/vt && chmod +x /usr/local/bin/vt

      - name: Sync to production
        env:
          VARTRACK_SERVER: ${{ vars.VARTRACK_SERVER }}
          VARTRACK_TOKEN:  ${{ secrets.VARTRACK_TOKEN }}
          VARTRACK_TENANT: myapp
        run: |
          vt sync \
            --file        configs/app.yaml \
            --datasource  mongo \
            --env         production \
            --wait \
            --label       "${{ github.ref_name }}@${{ github.sha }}"

docs.title: Multi-environment sync
docs.text:
strategy:
  matrix:
    include:
      - env: staging
        datasource: mongo-staging
      - env: production
        datasource: mongo-primary

steps:
  - name: Sync ${{ matrix.env }}
    env:
      VARTRACK_SERVER: ${{ vars.VARTRACK_SERVER }}
      VARTRACK_TOKEN:  ${{ secrets.VARTRACK_TOKEN }}
    run: |
      vt sync \
        --file       configs/app.yaml \
        --datasource ${{ matrix.datasource }} \
        --env        ${{ matrix.env }} \
        --wait

sync:production:
  stage: deploy
  environment: production
  only:
    - main
  script:
    - vt sync --file configs/app.yaml --datasource mongo --env production --wait
  when: manual

docs.title: Dry-run on every PR
docs.text:
Add a dry-run step to every PR to see exactly what would be written:

- name: Dry-run sync
  env:
    VARTRACK_SERVER: ${{ vars.VARTRACK_SERVER }}
    VARTRACK_TOKEN:  ${{ secrets.VARTRACK_TOKEN }}
  run: |
    vt sync \
      --file        configs/app.yaml \
      --datasource  mongo \
      --env         production \
      --dry-run \
      --wait \
      --json

Nothing is written. The task's message says how many keys each file would write and how its schema validation went — dry run — would write configs/app.yaml: 19 keys, validation ok — and the step fails when the task fails.

docs.title: Using environment variables
docs.text:
No vt login needed in CI/CD — just set the environment variables:

Variable Where to store VARTRACK_SERVER Repository variable (vars.VARTRACK_SERVER) VARTRACK_TOKEN Repository secret (secrets.VARTRACK_TOKEN) — a Git personal access token of a user or bot with push access to the rule's repositories (GitHub's built-in GITHUB_TOKEN cannot be used: it cannot read /user) VARTRACK_TENANT Repository variable or hardcoded in the workflow

docs.title: How varTrack Works
docs.text: varTrack is built around a simple idea: your Git repository is the source of truth for configuration, and any datasource that holds config values should automatically stay in sync with it.

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
Every sync — whether triggered by a webhook or the CLI — runs through the same pipeline. A CLI sync brings the file itself, so it skips fetching from Git: it starts at the rule for its datasource and goes straight to parsing.

PAYLOAD       →   ETL             →   SYNC
──────────────────────────────────────────────
resolve rule      fetch from Git      pick strategy
match platform    parse file          write to sinks
                  flatten keys        prune stale keys
                  validate CUE        rollback on error

docs.title: Stage 1 — Payload
docs.text:
When a webhook arrives at the gateway-service, varTrack resolves:

  • Which platform sent the event (GitHub, GitLab, ...)
  • Which rule applies: the one for the platform that sent the event and the datasource in the webhook URL (a rule is identified by that pair). Its repositories and exclude_repositories decide whether the pushed repository is synced, and file_name or file_path_map which files
  • Which environment to target (from branch name, PR number, tag, or explicit branch_map)

docs.title: Stage 2 — ETL
docs.text:
The orchestrator-service:

  1. Reads the files at the pushed commit, from a bare mirror of the repository kept under GIT_CACHE_DIR (at most 20 repos, least recently used removed first)
  2. Parses the file (YAML / JSON / TOML / .env / HCL / XML / INI)
  3. Extracts the subtree under the vartrack root key (if present)
  4. Detects the environment key pattern (branch-keyed or flat)
  5. Flattens nested config to { "key.subkey": "value" } using Rust BFS/DFS
  6. Applies variables_map overlay if configured
  7. Validates against the CUE schema for this tenant

docs.title: Stage 3 — Sync
docs.text:
Writes the validated flat map to every configured sink:

  • Picks the sync strategy (AUTO, GIT_UPSERT_ALL, GIT_SMART_REPAIR, or LIVE_STATE)
  • Runs writes to all matching sinks in parallel
  • Prunes stale keys once per environment, after all its files are written, if prune is enabled on the rule
  • Rolls back (deletes written data) if a write fails partway through

docs.title: Services
docs.text: Service Language Port Role gateway-service Go 5657 HTTP webhook receiver, platform routing, gRPC forwarder orchestrator-service Python + Rust 8000 / 50051 ETL pipeline, CUE validation, multi-sink writer watcher-service Go 9091 Drift detection, self-heal trigger vt Go — CLI for manual sync and CI/CD

docs.title: Rust core
docs.text:
Hot-path operations (flattening, merging, diffing, hashing) are implemented in Rust and exposed to Python via PyO3. Pure-Python fallbacks activate automatically if the Rust extension is not compiled — so the service always works, just slightly slower without it.

Module Purpose flatten BFS / DFS nested dict → flat key.subkey map merge Variable map overlay + environment resolution sync BLAKE3 content hash for GIT_SMART_REPAIR

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Destination template — control where data lands per rule
  • Environment resolution — map branches, PRs, and tags to environments
  • Sync strategies — choose how writes are applied
  • Drift detection — how the watcher catches and heals config drift

docs.title: Destination Template
docs.text: destination_template is a rule-level field that controls exactly where data lands in each sink — the collection name, key prefix, znode path, file path, or release name — using placeholders resolved at sync time.

docs.title: Placeholders
docs.text: Placeholder Resolved from {env} Resolved environment (e.g. production, staging, pr-42) {tenant} The tenant the rule belongs to: the tenant whose bundle.json layers it, or the repository owner when the rule names none

docs.title: Per-sink behavior
docs.text: Sink What it controls Template Resolved value MongoDB Collection name "{env}-config" production-config ZooKeeper znode root path "/{tenant}/{env}" /acme/pr-42 Redis Key prefix "{env}:cfg" production:cfg S3 Key prefix "{tenant}/{env}/" acme/production/ Linux server Full remote file path "/etc/app/{env}.env" /etc/app/production.env Helm Release name "app-{env}" app-production ConfigMap ConfigMap name "myapp-{env}" myapp-production Vercel Environment variable prefix "{env}_" production_

docs.title: One template, three environments
docs.text:
rules: [{
  platform:             "github"
  datasource:           "mongo"
  file_name:            "configs/app.yaml"
  repositories:         ["my-org/*"]
  destination_template: "{env}-config"
  branch_map: {
    main:    "production"
    develop: "staging"
    test:    "test"
  }
}]
Push branch Resolved env Collection written to main production production-config develop staging staging-config test test test-config

docs.title: Per-tenant isolation
docs.text:
destination_template: "{tenant}/{env}-config"

A push from tenant acme to main writes to acme/production-config. A push from tenant globex to main writes to globex/production-config.

docs.title: PR preview environments
docs.text:
rules: [{
  platform:             "github"
  datasource:           "mongo"
  file_name:            "configs/app.yaml"
  repositories:         ["my-org/app"]
  destination_template: "{env}-config"
  pr_as_env:            true    // PR #42 → env = "pr-42"
}]

Each pull request gets its own isolated collection: pr-42-config, pr-103-config, etc.

docs.title: ZooKeeper path per tenant and environment
docs.text:
rules: [{
  platform:             "github"
  datasource:           "zookeeper"
  destination_template: "/{tenant}/{env}"
}]

Writes znodes under /acme/production/, /acme/staging/, etc.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
If {env} appears in the template, at least one environment resolution strategy must be enabled:

  • branch_as_env: true
  • pr_as_env: true
  • tag_as_env: true
  • branch_map: { ... }
  • file_path_map: { ... }

varTrack will reject the bundle at startup if {env} is used with no resolution strategy configured.

docs.title: Fallback behavior
docs.text: If destination_template is not set, each sink falls back to its own sink-specific configuration key (e.g. collection for MongoDB, key_prefix for Redis).

docs.title: Drift Detection & Self-Heal
docs.text: For every rule with self_heal: true, the watcher-service asks the orchestrator on each poll whether the datasource still matches Git, and has it restore the ones that don't.

docs.title: What is drift?
docs.text:
Drift happens when a datasource value no longer matches what Git says it should be. Common causes:

  • A developer edits MongoDB directly during an incident
  • A deployment script overwrites a config value
  • A Kubernetes operator changes a ConfigMap
  • A Redis key expires or is flushed

Without drift detection, these changes go unnoticed until something breaks.

docs.title: How detection works
docs.text:
The orchestrator is the one component that reads and writes the sinks: it holds their credentials and their client code. So it also does the comparing. On every poll the watcher calls CheckDatasource; the orchestrator reads, in each synced environment, the keys varTrack wrote and compares them with what it last synced from Git (the sync ledger). The watcher itself reads no sink and holds no sink credentials.

Every POLL_INTERVAL (default: 60s), for each self_heal rule
  │
  └── CheckDatasource → the orchestrator reads the sink, key by key
        ├── in sync  → nothing to do
        ├── syncing  → a sync is still writing: look again on the next poll
        ├── unknown  → can't tell (never synced, sink unreadable): no heal
        └── drifted  → vartrack_watcher_drift_detected_total + 1
              └── Heal: SyncDatasource → the orchestrator re-syncs this
                  datasource from the head of every branch that feeds it

A few rules keep this from healing what it shouldn't, or waiting forever:

  • Unknown is not drift. A sink that cannot be read answers unknown, never "every key is missing", so an outage does not set off heals. A value the sink never gives back — a Vercel sensitive variable — is neither missing nor changed.
  • One heal at a time. After it asks for a heal, the watcher waits two poll intervals (at least 30 s) before asking again for the same drift, so the queued sync has time to start; a check that answers in sync ends the wait.
  • A failed heal is tried again on the next poll; while heal requests keep failing, a circuit breaker stops sending them for a while.
  • A sync that died — a worker killed mid-sync leaves no result. A sync still marked running after 15 minutes (Celery stops any task after 10) no longer counts, so the watcher heals instead of waiting on it.

docs.title: Enabling self-heal
docs.text:
Set self_heal: true on a rule to enable automatic repair:

rules: [{
  platform:   "github"
  datasource: "mongo"
  self_heal:  true    // watcher will restore state on drift
}]

The watcher asks the orchestrator which rules to watch on every poll, so a rule that gains self_heal, or is suspended or removed, is picked up at the next poll, without restarting the watcher. Rules with self_heal: false (or omitted) are not polled by the watcher, and nothing repairs them. The web UI still compares them with Git whenever it reads them, so their drift shows there until someone syncs from Git:

docs.title: Concrete example
docs.text:
Your config in Git:

max_connections: 50
log_level: info

Someone runs db.variables.updateOne({key: "max_connections"}, {$set: {value: 5}}) directly in MongoDB.

On the next poll cycle:

  1. The watcher asks the orchestrator (CheckDatasource): Git says 50, MongoDB has 5 — drifted
  2. self_heal: true → it calls SyncDatasource on the orchestrator
  3. The orchestrator fetches the file from Git, parses it, writes max_connections = 50 back to MongoDB
  4. The next check answers in sync — state restored

Had the change come from a push to Git, the sync of that push would have recorded it, step 1 would have answered in sync, and nothing would be healed.

Total recovery time: up to one POLL_INTERVAL (default 60 seconds).

On the web UI's Events page a repair shows as Healed. Drift on rules without self-heal shows as Drift detected and stays until someone syncs:

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Monitor drift in Prometheus / Grafana:

Metric Type Description vartrack_watcher_up Gauge 1 while a rule's loop runs

vartrack_watcher_drift_detected_total, vartrack_watcher_heal_triggered_total, vartrack_watcher_heal_failed_total and vartrack_watcher_poll_duration_seconds are registered, but the current watcher does not record them: they stay at zero. Follow drift with the web UI's Environments page and the DriftDetected, HealSucceeded and HealFailed events. All metrics are in Monitoring.

docs.title: Poll interval
docs.text:
Adjust how often the watcher checks each datasource:

POLL_INTERVAL=30s go run ./watcher-service/cmd

Lower values mean faster drift detection but more load on the orchestrator, which reads every self-heal datasource each poll.

docs.title: Why polling? (and how it's kept efficient)
docs.text:
varTrack uses a scheduled pull model rather than event-driven push because it must support eight fundamentally different backends — MongoDB, Redis, ZooKeeper, S3, Kubernetes ConfigMaps, Helm, Vercel, and Linux servers. Each backend exposes a different (or no) change-notification mechanism:

Datasource Native change events? MongoDB Change Streams (replica set only) Redis Keyspace notifications (off by default, extra config) ZooKeeper Watches (per-znode, limited concurrency) S3 Event notifications (requires SNS/SQS wiring) Linux server None — SSH file stat only Vercel None ConfigMap Kubernetes informer (requires in-cluster) Helm None — release state only

A unified polling model means a single code path works across all backends with no external infrastructure requirements.

How the overhead is minimised:

  • Lightweight reads — the orchestrator reads only the keys varTrack wrote in each environment, not the entire datasource, and reads the environments of a datasource in parallel.
  • Configurable interval — default 60 s; set POLL_INTERVAL to match your SLA.
  • Leader election — in multi-replica deployments, only one replica polls (ZooKeeper or Redis distributed lock).
  • Circuit breaker — while heal requests keep failing, the watcher stops sending them for a while.

docs.title: Multi-replica deployments
docs.text:
When running multiple watcher replicas, only one should poll and heal at a time. Leader election ensures this:

bundle: {
  watcher_leader_election_datasource: "redis"   // or "zookeeper"
}

This is the only thing the watcher reads config.cue for. The datasource is one of the bundle's datasources, named like the others (redis, or redis-broker for the one tagged broker). Its password may be written inline or as a {file: …}; a {ref: …} is refused at startup, because the watcher has no secret manager.

Replicas that are not the leader stay idle. If the leader crashes, another replica acquires the lock within one TTL window (15 seconds for Redis).

The watcher keeps no state between polls: the orchestrator compares with its sync ledger. (watcher_state_datasource was removed; a config.cue that still sets it loads, with a log line.)

docs.title: Environment Resolution
docs.text:
When a webhook fires, varTrack resolves a single environment string from the event. This string is used to:

  • Resolve {env} in destination_template
  • Select the correct subtree from env-keyed config files
  • Determine which sink collection, prefix, or path to write to

docs.title: Resolution order
docs.text:
varTrack tries each strategy in order and uses the first one that produces a match:

Priority Strategy Example 1 branch_map[branch] main → production 2 file_path_map[file_path] configs/prod/** → production 3 pr_as_env: true PR #42 → pr-42 4 branch_as_env: true branch develop → develop 5 tag_as_env: true tag v1.2.3 → v1.2.3 6 fallback always → default

pr_as_env, branch_as_env and tag_as_env used to be called env_as_pr, env_as_branch and env_as_tags (and the S3 option prefix_as_env was env_as_prefix). The old names still work in config.cue, bundle.json and vartrack.json; varTrack logs a warning with the new name.

docs.title: branch_map — explicit mapping
docs.text:
Map specific branch names to environment names:

rules: [{
  platform:   "github"
  datasource: "mongo"
  branch_map: {
    main:    "production"
    develop: "staging"
    qa:      "qa"
  }
}]

Pushes to main write to production-config. Pushes to develop write to staging-config. Any branch not in the map falls through to the next strategy.

The web UI's Environments page lists every resolved environment with the branch it comes from and where it is written:

docs.title: file_path_map — path glob mapping
docs.text:
Map file paths (glob patterns) to environment names:

rules: [{
  platform:   "github"
  datasource: "mongo"
  file_path_map: {
    "configs/production/**": "production"
    "configs/staging/**":    "staging"
  }
}]

A push that changes configs/production/app.yaml resolves to production.

docs.title: pr_as_env — PR environments
docs.text:
pr_as_env: true

Pull request events resolve to pr-{number}. Useful for ephemeral preview environments.

PR #42  → env = "pr-42"
PR #103 → env = "pr-103"

docs.title: branch_as_env — branch name as environment
docs.text:
branch_as_env: true

The branch name becomes the environment name directly:

branch "develop"     → env = "develop"
branch "feature/foo" → env = "feature/foo"

docs.title: tag_as_env — tag name as environment
docs.text:
tag_as_env: true

Tag push events use the tag name as the environment:

tag "v1.2.3"    → env = "v1.2.3"
tag "release-5" → env = "release-5"

docs.title: root_key — extracting a subtree before slicing
docs.text:
If your config file has a wrapper key, set root_key in the rule to unwrap it first. varTrack extracts the subtree under that key, then runs env auto-detection on it.

rules: [{
  root_key: "vartrack"   // default — extract the "vartrack" subtree if it exists
}]

# configs/app.yaml
vartrack:
  production:
    database_host: mongo.prod.internal
  staging:
    database_host: mongo.staging.internal
other_tool:
  setting: ignored      # not under root_key — never touched

root_key: "vartrack" → extracts the inner dict → Pattern 1 runs on it → database_host=mongo.prod.internal for production.

Set root_key: "" to always process the whole file regardless of structure.

If the key doesn't exist in the file, varTrack soft-falls back to the whole file.

docs.title: Auto-detection from config file structure
docs.text: When your config file itself is keyed by environment, varTrack auto-detects the structure and extracts only the relevant slice — no extra rule config needed. Three patterns are supported.

docs.title: Pattern 1 — all top-level keys are env names
docs.text:
Every top-level value is a dict. varTrack merges default first, then the matching env overrides it.

# configs/app.yaml
production:
  database_host: mongo.prod.internal
  max_connections: 100
staging:
  database_host: mongo.staging.internal
  max_connections: 10
default:
  max_connections: 5    # fallback for unknown envs
  log_level: info
env result production database_host=mongo.prod.internal, max_connections=100, log_level=info staging database_host=mongo.staging.internal, max_connections=10, log_level=info pr-42 max_connections=5, log_level=info (from default)

docs.title: Pattern 2 — per-field env sub-keys mixed with scalars
docs.text:
Each field that varies per env has a dict of env→value. Fields that are the same across all envs are plain scalars.

# configs/app.yaml
database_host:
  production: mongo.prod.internal
  staging:    mongo.staging.internal
  default:    mongo.local
max_connections: 50     # same for every env — written as-is
log_level: info
env result production database_host=mongo.prod.internal, max_connections=50, log_level=info staging database_host=mongo.staging.internal, max_connections=50, log_level=info pr-42 database_host=mongo.local, max_connections=50, log_level=info

docs.title: Pattern 3 — env dicts and scalar defaults at the same level
docs.text:
Some keys at the same nesting level are env names (dicts with overrides), others are plain scalars that apply to every env. Order in the file doesn't matter — varTrack categorizes by value type, not position. The env dict is merged on top of the scalars.

{
    "production": { "name": "worn",  "db": "mongo.prod.internal" },
    "predev":     { "name": "dan",   "db": "mongo.dev.internal"  },
    "name":       "bob",
    "age":        33,
    "timeout":    30
}
env result production name=worn, db=mongo.prod.internal, age=33, timeout=30 predev name=dan, db=mongo.dev.internal, age=33, timeout=30 unknown (no match, no default dict) data returned unchanged

Add a default dict to handle unknown envs:

{
    "production": { "name": "worn" },
    "default":    { "name": "bob" },
    "age":        33
}

unknown env → name=bob, age=33.

docs.title: Pattern 3 — env-named top-level dicts mixed with scalar defaults
docs.text:
{
    "prod":   { "name": "worn" },
    "predev": { "name": "dan" },
    "name":   "bob",
    "age":    33
}

Top-level dicts whose key matches the resolved env are applied as overrides. Top-level scalars are universal defaults merged underneath:

env result prod name=worn, age=33 predev name=dan, age=33 unknown (no matching dict, no default dict) data returned unchanged

You can also include a default dict for unknown env fallback:

{
    "prod":    { "name": "worn" },
    "default": { "name": "bob" },
    "age":     33
}

unknown env → name=bob, age=33.

docs.title: default fallback
docs.text: In all three patterns, if the resolved env has no matching key, varTrack silently falls back to default. If there is no default either, the data is returned unchanged.

docs.title: root_key — extracting a subtree before slicing
docs.text:
Real config files often live alongside other tooling config (Spring, Maven, npm, etc.). Use root_key to extract only the varTrack-relevant subtree before env-detection runs.

rules: [{
  root_key: "vartrack"   // default — extract "vartrack" subtree if present
}]

Set root_key: "" to always process the whole file. If the key doesn't exist, varTrack soft-falls back to the whole file.

docs.title: Example — package.json
docs.text:
A Node.js project that also carries deploy config inside package.json:

{
  "name": "my-app",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "scripts": { "start": "node index.js" },
  "vartrack": {
    "production": { "API_URL": "https://api.prod.com",  "LOG_LEVEL": "warn"  },
    "staging":    { "API_URL": "https://api.stg.com",   "LOG_LEVEL": "info"  },
    "default":    { "API_URL": "https://api.local.com", "LOG_LEVEL": "debug" }
  }
}

rules: [{
  file_name: "package.json"
  root_key:  "vartrack"       // ignore name/version/scripts — only sync vartrack block
  branch_map: { main: "production", develop: "staging" }
}]

Push to main → API_URL=https://api.prod.com, LOG_LEVEL=warn written to the sink.

docs.title: Example — pom.xml (Maven)
docs.text:
A Java project with deploy properties in pom.xml. varTrack parses XML and extracts the subtree:

<project>
  <groupId>com.example</groupId>
  <artifactId>my-service</artifactId>

  <vartrack>
    <production>
      <database_host>mongo.prod.internal</database_host>
      <max_connections>100</max_connections>
    </production>
    <staging>
      <database_host>mongo.staging.internal</database_host>
      <max_connections>10</max_connections>
    </staging>
    <default>
      <max_connections>5</max_connections>
    </default>
  </vartrack>
</project>

rules: [{
  file_name: "pom.xml"
  root_key:  "vartrack"
  branch_map: { main: "production", develop: "staging" }
}]

Push to main → database_host=mongo.prod.internal, max_connections=100.

docs.title: Combining strategies
docs.text:
Strategies can be combined. varTrack uses the first one that matches:

rules: [{
  platform:   "github"
  datasource: "mongo"
  branch_map: {
    main:    "production"   // explicit — highest priority
    develop: "staging"
  }
  pr_as_env:     true       // fallback for PRs not in branch_map
  branch_as_env: true       // fallback for all other branches
}]
Event Resolved env Push to main production (from branch_map) Push to develop staging (from branch_map) PR #42 opened pr-42 (from pr_as_env) Push to feature/x feature/x (from branch_as_env)

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
The words varTrack's docs, logs and web UI use, and what each one means here.

Platform A Git server that sends varTrack push webhooks: an entry of platforms in config.cue (github, gitea, or {type}-{tag} such as gitea-team). It also answers who a caller is and what they may do, for the CLI API and the web UI. Datasource A place varTrack writes configuration to: an entry of datasources in config.cue (mongo, redis, s3-minio, …). Its block holds the connection settings and credentials. Each datasource type is written by a sink. Sink The code that writes one datasource type — MongoDB, Redis, ZooKeeper, S3, Kubernetes ConfigMap, Helm, Vercel, Linux server. See Sinks. Rule What is synced, from where, to where and how: one entry of rules in config.cue, named by its platform and datasource (at most one rule per pair). A tenant's bundle.json and a repository's vartrack.json can adjust it. See How a rule is built. Layer One of the files a rule is built from — config.cue, bundle.json, vartrack.json — plus config.cue's force, applied last. Each overrides the one before. Tenant A team with its own schema repository, registered with SCHEMA_TENANT_<ID>_REPO. Its bundle.json holds its layer of the rules, its CUE schemas validate its files, and the web UI shows each user the tenants' rules their Git account can read. A rule no tenant's bundle.json names belongs to tenant default. Schema repository (schema registry) A tenant's Git repository with bundle.json and the CUE schemas. See Schema registry. Config repository A repository whose pushes a rule syncs: it holds the configuration files (configs/app.yaml, …) and, optionally, a vartrack.json. Preset A JSON file of rule settings in any repository, pulled into a bundle.json or a vartrack.json with extends. See Presets. Environment The label a push is synced under — production, staging, pr-42, v1.2.0 — from the rule's branch_map, or the branch, PR number or tag. See Environment resolution. Target One environment of one datasource, for one tenant: the unit varTrack records state for, locks while writing, prunes and checks for drift. The web UI's Environments page lists targets. Desired state What Git says a target holds: the flat keys of the files last synced to it, kept per file in the sync ledger (Redis). Secrets are kept as digests, never as values. Flat key A value's path in its file, dot-separated: database.host, api.regions.0. Every file format is read as flat keys; a sink stores them as they are, or nested again (MongoDB's document strategy, the JSON structure of Redis). Key space Where in a store a target's keys land — a Redis hash or prefix, a ZooKeeper path, a Vercel target. Two targets with the same key space write the same keys; prune never deletes a key another target still holds there. Sync One run that reads the pushed files at the pushed commit, validates them, and writes them to the datasource: started by a push, by vt sync, by the web UI, or by self-heal. Each sync is a task. Prune Deleting keys varTrack wrote before that Git no longer holds, once per environment after its files are written. Only on sinks that keep each key separately. See What prune deletes. Drift A key whose value in the datasource differs from the desired state, or is missing. See Drift detection. Self-heal The watcher asking the orchestrator, on every poll, whether each self_heal rule's datasource still matches Git, and having it write Git's values back when it does not. Dry run A sync that reads, validates and reports everything but writes nothing. Shape How a MongoDB datasource stores a file: one document per key (STRATEGY_KEY_VALUE) or one document per file (STRATEGY_DOCUMENT, STRATEGY_FILE). Changing it replaces the other shape's documents and records a Shape changed event.

docs.title: Sync Strategies
docs.text: A sync strategy controls how varTrack applies the flattened config values to a datasource. The right strategy depends on the size of your config and how often you need reads vs. writes.

docs.title: Strategies
docs.text:
AUTO (recommended)GIT_UPSERT_ALLGIT_SMART_REPAIRLIVE_STATE

varTrack picks the strategy automatically based on payload size:

  • ≤ 500 keys → GIT_UPSERT_ALL

  • 500 keys → GIT_SMART_REPAIR

This is the default and works well for most configurations. No tuning needed.

sync_mode: "AUTO"

Writes every key from the flattened Git payload to the datasource in one bulk operation. Does not read the current state first.

Best for: Small configs (< 500 keys), initial bootstrapping, or when you always want a clean overwrite.

sync_mode: "SYNC_MODE_GIT_UPSERT_ALL"
Read before write No Keys written All Stale key cleanup Only if prune: true set Best for Small configs

Reads what the datasource holds first and writes only what differs. Uses BLAKE3 content hashing to detect unchanged values.

Only the MongoDB sink reads before writing: with STRATEGY_KEY_VALUE it writes the keys whose value changed, with a document strategy it rewrites the file's document when it was written from another commit. Every other sink writes every key, as with GIT_UPSERT_ALL.

Best for: Large configs (> 500 keys), or datasources where minimizing write operations matters.

sync_mode: "SYNC_MODE_GIT_SMART_REPAIR"
Read before write Yes Keys written Changed only Stale key cleanup Only if prune: true set Best for Large configs

Written like GIT_UPSERT_ALL: every key, without reading the datasource first. Keys Git no longer holds are deleted only by prune.

sync_mode: "SYNC_MODE_LIVE_STATE"

docs.title: Setting the strategy
docs.text:
Override per rule in config.cue:

rules: [{
  platform:   "github"
  datasource: "mongo"
  sync_mode:  "SYNC_MODE_GIT_SMART_REPAIR"
}]

Or let AUTO decide — just omit sync_mode or set it to "AUTO".

Each mode can be written short ("AUTO", "GIT_SMART_REPAIR") or as its full proto name ("SYNC_MODE_AUTO", "SYNC_MODE_GIT_SMART_REPAIR"); both load.

docs.title: Stale key pruning
docs.text:
When keys are removed from your Git config file, varTrack can delete them from the datasource:

rules: [{
  platform:   "github"
  datasource: "mongo"
  sync_mode:  "AUTO"
  prune:      true     // delete keys present in datasource but missing from Git
}]

Warning

prune: true permanently deletes keys from the datasource that are no longer in Git. Use prune: {enabled: true, dry_run: true} or the full dry-run first to verify what would be removed.

docs.title: What prune deletes
docs.text:
Prune runs once per environment, after all of its files are written, and only if none of them failed. So a key that moved from one file to another is never deleted, and there is nothing to configure for multi-file rules.

A key is stale when varTrack wrote it before and no file of the environment holds it any more. Prune deletes nothing else:

  • A key somebody else put in the datasource is never deleted, with or without protection.
  • A stale key that was changed outside varTrack since varTrack wrote it is kept, and reported with a PruneSkipped event.
  • Environments that write to the same place keep each other's keys: Vercel's staging and develop both write to preview, and a Redis key_prefix or a ZooKeeper path without {env} is shared by every environment.
  • So do datasources and tenants. A datasource's name says nothing about where it writes. Two datasources on the same Redis database (same servers and db) with the same key_prefix and hash, the same ZooKeeper servers and root path, or the same Vercel team, project and targets write the same keys, and one never prunes a key the other still holds. A datasource on another server, or with another prefix, is not compared. MongoDB filters its documents by tenant, datasource and environment, so its datasources never share keys. Who holds a key is recorded with each sync, as the key space the sync wrote to, so another tenant counts even when its schema repository cannot be read right now. A target last written by an older version has no such record and is placed by the rules until it is written again. When a prune finds another target holding keys in the same key space, the UI shows one Shared key space warning event for the environment (again after the sharing has ended and begun anew).
  • If the rules of the tenants cannot be listed when prune runs, nothing is pruned, as when the ledger cannot be read.
  • If the delete fails, the sync still succeeds. The keys stay on the list and the next sync retries them (a PruneFailed event).

Prune applies to sinks that keep each key separately: Redis (hash or strings), Vercel, ZooKeeper and MongoDB with update_strategy: "STRATEGY_KEY_VALUE". A sink that replaces a whole object on every write — ConfigMap, S3, Linux server, Helm, MongoDB with its default STRATEGY_DOCUMENT (or STRATEGY_FILE), Redis with the JSON structure — has no stale key to delete. Setting prune on one has no effect.

prune.last was removed: the delete is always last now. A prune block that only had last is a disabled block; write prune: true or prune: {enabled: true}.

docs.title: prune.protection
docs.text:
Glob patterns for keys that must never be deleted, even if they're absent from Git. A pattern is matched against the flat key, like db.host, before the sink formats it for its own layout:

rules: [{
  prune: {
    enabled:    true
    protection: ["SYSTEM_*", "_vt_*", "readonly.*"]
  }
}]

prune_protection, the former flat name, is still read from bundle.json and vartrack.json; config.cue only takes the prune block.

docs.title: Full dry-run — simulate the entire sync
docs.text:
No writes, no deletes. Returns a full report of what would be written, changed, and deleted. The keys prune would see as stale are listed per environment under prune.would_delete; whether something changed one outside varTrack is only known when a real sync reads it.

# Via CLI
vt sync --file configs/app.yaml --datasource mongo --env staging --dry-run

# Via HTTP
POST /v1/webhooks/mongo/dry-run

@secret-annotated fields are fetched from Vault but masked as *** in the report.

In the web UI, Dry run on a rule runs the same simulation for the environments you pick:

docs.title: Prune dry-run — simulate deletes only
docs.text:
Test the prune step independently without touching any writes. Enabled per rule:

rules: [{
  prune: {
    enabled: true
    dry_run: true   // always simulate deletes — never actually remove keys
  }
}]

With prune.dry_run, every sync runs normally (writes go through) but the delete step is always simulated, never executed. The task reports the stale keys, and they stay on the list: turn dry_run off and the next sync deletes them.

docs.title: Configuration files
docs.text: varTrack is configured by a few files, each in a different place and owned by a different team. This page says which file holds what, where it lives, who edits it, and how the files combine into the rule a sync runs with.

docs.text:
File Lives in Edited by Read by Picked up config.cue The hosts that run varTrack, at the path in CONFIG_PATH; every service mounts the same file The team that runs varTrack gateway, orchestrator, watcher orchestrator: the next time it reads the file after it changed. gateway: when it starts, so restart it after changing platforms or rules. watcher: when it starts, for its leader election only — it gets the rules from the orchestrator bundle.json (or rules.json) The root of a tenant's schema repository The tenant orchestrator First use, then every SCHEMA_TTL_SECONDS (300 s), and at once on a push to that repository CUE schemas (*.cue) The same schema repository The tenant orchestrator, before a file is written As bundle.json vartrack.json A config repository (the one that is pushed): vartrack.json, .github/vartrack.json, .gitea/vartrack.json or .gitlab/vartrack.json, the first found The repository's owners orchestrator On every sync, at the pushed commit Presets Any repository a file names in extends Whoever owns that repository orchestrator With the file that extends them SCHEMA_TENANT_<ID>_REPO / _BRANCH / _TOKEN The environment of the orchestrator API and its workers The team that runs varTrack orchestrator When it starts ~/.config/vt/config.yaml The machine that runs vt Each user (vt login, vt config) vt On every command 
flowchart LR

        CUE["config.cue<br/>platforms · datasources · rules · force"]
    end

One file per job

config.cue decides what exists — which platforms send pushes, which datasources can be written and how to reach them, which rules there are, and what no one else may change. bundle.json and vartrack.json only adjust those rules for a tenant and for a repository. Nothing in them repeats config.cue, so nothing has to be kept in step.

docs.title: How a rule is built
docs.text:
A sync looks up the rule for the push's platform and datasource and builds it in layers. Each layer overrides the one before it, option by option:

  1. config.cue — the rule as the team running varTrack wrote it.
  2. bundle.json — the tenant's settings for the same platform and datasource.
  3. vartrack.json — the pushed repository's settings, read at the pushed commit.
  4. force — the config.cue rule's force block, applied last: what no tenant or repository may change.

A bundle.json or vartrack.json can pull in shared settings with extends. The presets are part of that file's layer: they are resolved first, and the file's own settings go on top of them.

Every other option is replaced by the layer above it. Two kinds behave differently.

docs.title: Merged options
docs.text:
These combine key by key, so a layer adds to them instead of replacing them: a bundle.json branch_map of {develop: staging} adds to config.cue's {main: production}. prune.protection patterns add up across layers — a layer can protect more keys, never fewer.

  • branch_map
  • file_path_map
  • prune
  • variables_map

docs.title: Options only config.cue sets
docs.text:
These decide which repositories a rule covers, where secrets come from and who may change what, so a lower layer cannot change them. In bundle.json they are dropped with a warning; in vartrack.json they are ignored and logged.

  • exclude_repositories
  • force
  • overrides
  • repositories
  • secret_manager
  • self_heal
  • tenants

A datasource's connection settings — its endpoint, database, bucket, host and credentials — come only from its datasource block in config.cue.

Which option may be set in which file is listed for every option in the Rule options reference.

docs.title: An example: three files, one rule
Check a file before you push it
docs.text:
File Check Where config.cue vt bundle validate config.cue locally; the gateway also refuses to start on a field the bundle does not have your machine, CI bundle.json, vartrack.json vt validate-config — with no file named it checks the vartrack.json files of the current directory; exits 1 on errors or warnings, and with --strict also on renamed options the config repository's CI (example) A config file against its CUE schema vt validate --file configs/app.yaml --datasource mongo CI, before merging

A file that cannot be used stops the sync instead of being half-applied: a vartrack.json that is not valid JSON fails its sync, and a bundle.json that does not parse leaves the tenant without rules until it is fixed (see Presets).

docs.title: CUE Schema Annotations
docs.text: varTrack supports two custom annotations in CUE schema files: @secret() and @logger(). Both are declared on fields in your schema, not in your config files.

docs.title: @secret()
docs.text: Marks a field whose value is a Vault path at ETL time instead of a real value. Before writing to any sink, the orchestrator reads the schema, finds every @secret-annotated field, fetches the real value from Vault, and injects it in-place.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
// default secret manager
"db.password": string @secret()

// named secret manager (matches secret_managers[].vault tag in the bundle)
"api_key": string @secret(ref="other-vault")

docs.title: Config file side
docs.text:
In the actual config file being synced (YAML, JSON, TOML, etc.) the field value is the Vault path:

# configs/app.yaml
database:
  password: "@secret(secret/myapp/db#password)"

auth:
  jwt_secret: "@secret(secret/myapp/auth#jwt_secret)"

The format is @secret(mount/path#field) — mount path + # + field name inside the Vault secret.

docs.title: What happens at ETL time
docs.text:
1. Parse schema → find @secret-annotated fields
2. For each field present in flat_data:
   a. Determine secret manager: ref= or "default"
   b. Fetch value from Vault: the path and field from "@secret(mount/path#field)"
      (the manager's mount point may lead the path)
   c. Replace flat_data[field] with the real value
3. Write to sink — Vault value arrives, not the path string

docs.title: Dry-run behaviour
docs.text: In dry-run mode, @secret fields are masked as *** in the report. The real value is fetched from Vault but never returned to the caller.

docs.title: Bundle wiring
docs.text:
The ref= value must match the tag of a secret manager declared in the bundle:

bundle: {
  secret_managers: [
    {
      vault: {
        tag:         "default"   // matched by @secret()
        endpoint:    "https://vault.mycompany.com"
        mount_point: "secret"
        kv_version:  2
        token_auth: { token: "hvs.xxxx" }
      }
    },
    {
      vault: {
        tag:         "other-vault"   // matched by @secret(ref="other-vault")
        endpoint:    "https://vault2.mycompany.com"
        mount_point: "secret"
        kv_version:  2
        token_auth: { token: "hvs.yyyy" }
      }
    },
  ]
}

@secret() without ref= uses the rule's secret_manager when it names one, else the entry tagged default, else the bundle's only one. Secret managers are declared in config.cue's secret_managers only; a rule's own secrets block was removed. A field whose value is not in the @secret(path#field) form is read at the manager's path_prefix, under the field's own name.

docs.title: @logger()
docs.text: Marks a field for structured change logging. Every time a value changes between ETL runs, the orchestrator emits an INFO log entry showing the field name, old value, new value, datasource, and environment.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
app_port:      int    @logger()
database.host: string @logger()

docs.title: Log output
docs.text:
When a non-secret field changes:

field changed  datasource=mongo  env=production  field=app_port
               from=8080  to=9090  file=configs/app.yaml

When a field is written for the first time (no old value):

field changed  datasource=mongo  env=production  field=database.host
               to="db.prod.internal"  file=configs/app.yaml

docs.title: Combining with @secret()
docs.text:
You can annotate a field with both. The change is logged but the values are never revealed — only changed=true is recorded:

"database.password": string @secret() @logger()

field changed  datasource=mongo  env=production  field=database.password
               changed=true  file=configs/app.yaml

docs.title: Full schema example
docs.text:
// app.yaml.cue at the root of the schema repo — checks every file named app.yaml
"app.port":          string & =~"^[0-9]+$"   @logger()
"log.level":         "debug" | "info" | "warn" | "error"
"database.host":     string & !=""            @logger()
"database.port":     string & =~"^[0-9]+$"   @logger()
"database.password": string & !=""            @secret() @logger()
"api.secret_key":    string & !=""            @secret()
"max_connections"?:  string & =~"^[0-9]+$"

The fields are at the top level, not inside a #Definition — cue vet checks the data only against top-level fields. Values are strings, as the file is flattened first, so a number is a string matching a pattern; see CUE schemas.

Register the schema in your bundle:

bundle: {
  schema_registry: {
    platform: "github"
    repo:     "my-org/schemas"
    branch:   "main"
  }
  // ...
}

varTrack fetches the schema from Git, runs cue vet to validate the payload, then processes @secret and @logger annotations before writing to any sink.

docs.title: Authentication & Authorization
docs.text: varTrack's CLI API (/v1/cli/*, used by vt) keeps no users or roles of its own. The caller shows their own Git token, and the rule's Git platform says what they may do. An optional OPA policy then decides with the whole request.

docs.title: Git permissions
docs.text:
vt sends the caller's Git token for the rule's platform — a GitHub or Gitea personal access token — as Authorization: Bearer <token>:

vt login --server https://gateway.example.com --token <your Git token>

For each request the gateway asks the platform of the rule that syncs to the datasource who the token belongs to (GET /user) and what they may do in the rule's repositories (GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}, and GET /user/repos for patterns such as acme/*):

The caller can, in one of the rule's repositories… …so they may push vt sync read vt sync --dry-run, vt validate, vt task

A rule's repositories are the ones its repositories and enabled overrides name or match, minus its exclusions — the repositories the gateway routes pushes from. The web UI decides the same way (see below).

Answer When 401 no token, or the platform rejects it 403 the caller lacks the access above, or the OPA policy denies the request 404 no rule syncs to the datasource; a task of a rule the caller cannot read

vt validate without --datasource, and vt validate-config, need a token any platform of the bundle accepts. vt task list shows the tasks of the rules the caller can read.

The platform:login entries of ui.auth.admins may do anything, on the CLI API as in the UI. Tasks record their caller as login@platform.

The bundle's auth.oidc and auth.rbac blocks are no longer used; the gateway logs a warning when they are set.

docs.title: OPA — policy layer (Open Policy Agent)
docs.text:
OPA runs after the Git permission check for decisions Git permissions can't express — e.g., "writers may sync anywhere but production". Give the policy in exactly one of three ways:

auth: {
  opa: {
    inline_policy: """
      package vartrack.authz

      default allow = false

      # validate and task reads: Git read access has decided
      allow {
        input.action != "sync"
      }

      # anyone who may push syncs outside production
      allow {
        input.action == "sync"
        input.env    != "production"
      }

      # only repository admins sync production
      allow {
        input.action == "sync"
        input.env    == "production"
        input.user.permission == "admin"
      }
    """

    // policy_file: "/etc/vartrack/policy.rego"                      // a file on the gateway
    // server_url:  "http://opa:8181/v1/data/vartrack/authz/allow"  // a remote OPA server
  }
}

The policy must be in package vartrack.authz and define allow; anything but allow == true denies the request. Policies are written in Rego v0 syntax (allow { … }), as above. To write Rego v1 syntax (allow if { … }, x in xs), start the policy with import rego.v1.

inline_policy and policy_file are compiled in-process (tens of microseconds per decision) — no OPA server required. With server_url the gateway asks that server instead: point it at the rule (…/v1/data/vartrack/authz/allow) or at the package (…/v1/data/vartrack/authz, whose allow is then read). A server that cannot be reached, answers anything but 2xx, or takes longer than five seconds denies the request with 500. A policy that does not compile, or a policy file that cannot be read, stops the gateway at startup.

A full example policy — admins sync anywhere, writers outside production but never configs/secrets/*, dry runs anywhere — is at examples/policies/vartrack_authz.rego.

docs.title: OPA input document
docs.text:
Every request evaluation receives:

Field Example input.user.login "alice" — on the rule's platform input.user.platform "gitea" input.user.permission "admin", "write" or "read" — in the rule's repositories input.user.admin true for ui.auth.admins entries input.user.repositories ["acme/configs"] — the rule's repository names and patterns input.action "sync", "validate" input.resource "datasource" input.datasource "mongo" input.env "production" (lower-cased) input.file_path "configs/app.yaml" input.tenant_id "acme" input.dry_run false

docs.title: Reloading the policy
docs.text: POST /admin/opa/reload on the gateway's admin port (ADMIN_ADDR, default :9090) recompiles the policy and re-reads policy_file. If the new policy does not compile, the call answers 422 with the compile error and the previous policy stays in force. A policy_file is also re-read every OPA_RELOAD_INTERVAL (default 30m).

docs.title: Layer evaluation order
docs.text:
Request
  │
  ▼
Git token             ← 401 if missing, or the rule's platform rejects it
  │
  ▼
Git permission        ← 403 without push (sync) or read (anything else) access
  │
  ▼
OPA evaluation        ← 403 if the policy does not allow it
  │
  ▼
Handler

OPA is skipped if no opa block is configured.

docs.title: Web UI sign-in with your Git platform
docs.text:
The web UI can sign users in with the Git platforms your rules already use (GitHub, GitHub Enterprise, Gitea) and show each user only what those platforms let them see. varTrack keeps no list of who may see what: each rule is judged on its own platform, asked with the user's own account there.

The user can, on the rule's platform… …so in the UI they read at least one repository the rule covers see the rule, its tasks and its events read the repository an environment was last synced from see that environment, its keys and its diff write to one of the rule's repositories can Sync it; with read access only they can Dry run it

A rule covers the repositories it names, the ones its patterns (acme/*) match minus its exclusions, and the ones its environments were synced from. A rule, environment or task the user cannot see answers not found, exactly like one that does not exist. Answers are cached for two minutes per session, so a permission change on a platform shows up within that time.

docs.title: Tenants are shown, not chosen
docs.text:
The UI covers every tenant at once: a rule, task or event carries its tenant, and what a person sees is what Git lets them read, whichever tenant it belongs to. There is no tenant to switch to.

Who Sees Sign-in is off every rule of every tenant An admin (ui.auth.admins) every rule of every tenant A signed-in user every rule, of any tenant, whose repository their account can read on the rule's platform. A tenant with no such rule does not appear at all.

When the viewer sees more than one tenant, the Rules, Environments, Events and Tasks pages show the tenant and offer a Tenant filter that lists only those tenants. The same platform/datasource can exist in two tenants, so a rule is identified by its tenant too: /rules/{tenant}/{platform}/{datasource}; a link without the tenant still opens the rule when only one visible tenant has it.

A rule you cannot see because you have not connected its platform is counted, never named: the Rules page says "3 rules on gitea are hidden" with a Connect gitea button. Rules on a platform you are connected to, in repositories your account cannot read, are not counted — that would show that a private repository's rules exist.

The UI API takes an optional ?tenant= (or the X-Tenant-ID header) to narrow an answer to one tenant. It narrows only: it never shows a rule the viewer cannot read.

docs.title: Rules on several platforms
docs.text: With rules on GitHub and on Gitea, add a provider for each. Users sign in with either one and connect the other from the sign-in page, the user menu or their profile — the same session then holds both accounts, and each rule is judged with the account on its own platform. A GitHub rule is never judged by a Gitea account, even when the repository names match. Until a platform is connected, its rules stay hidden and the UI says how many there are. Signing out ends the session on every platform. Rules on a platform without sign-in set up are hidden from everyone but admins.

docs.title: Set it up
docs.text:
1. Register an OAuth application on each platform, all with the same callback URL: {public_url}/api/orchestrator/v1/auth/callback — for example http://localhost:8080/api/orchestrator/v1/auth/callback.
    • GitHub: Settings → Developer settings → OAuth Apps. GitHub OAuth Apps can only read private repositories with the repo scope, which is the default here.
    • Gitea: Settings → Applications → OAuth2 Applications, confidential client. Default scopes: read:user read:repository.
  2. Add a ui block to the bundle (config.cue), with one provider per platform users sign in with:
bundle: {
  platforms: [
    {github: {endpoint: "https://github.com", ...}},
    {gitea:  {endpoint: "http://gitea:3000", ...}},
  ]

  ui: {
    public_url: "https://vartrack.example.com"   // where users open the UI
    auth: {
      providers: [
        {
          platform:      "github"                // a platform's name from platforms
          client_id:     "Iv1.8a61f9b3a7aba766"
          client_secret: {file: "/run/secrets/github-oauth"}
        },
        {
          platform:      "gitea"
          client_id:     {file: "/run/secrets/gitea-oauth-id"}
          client_secret: {ref: {path: "ui/gitea", key: "client_secret"}}   // from Vault
          browser_url:   "https://gitea.example.com"   // when the platform's endpoint is internal
        },
      ]
      admins: ["github:octo-admin"]              // optional: see and sync every rule
      secret_manager: "vault"                    // optional with a single secret manager
    }
  }
}
Field Default Description ui.public_url http://localhost:5173 Where users open the UI; the callback is built from it ui.auth.providers[].platform — A platform's name from platforms: github, gitea, gitea-team… ui.auth.providers[].client_id / client_secret — The OAuth application: a string, {value: "…"}, {file: "/path"} or {ref: {path: "…", key: "…"}} ui.auth.providers[].browser_url the platform's endpoint The platform's address as the browser sees it, when the endpoint is internal (e.g. http://gitea:3000) ui.auth.providers[].scopes per platform, see above OAuth scopes ui.auth.admins — platform:login entries that see every rule; with one provider a bare login works.
